passage:
I'm Salma, Kiran's flatmate, and here's what I noticed over a month.

Kiran started following a loud creator who talks about rents and how hard life is for young people. He says things Kiran has said for years. When his videos play, Kiran grins, leans forward and repeats his sharpest lines. When he mocks a named person, Kiran laughs out loud. It looks thrilling.

But afterwards Kiran is wound up, jaw tight, snapping at small things. The videos end with links to his paid channel and merchandise.

Last week I asked, "Who makes money when you're angry?" Kiran didn't answer straight away. Then Kiran said, "The rent stuff is good, though." I think that's true. This week Kiran muted the live chat but kept watching.

qa.q: What does the creator talk about?
qa.a: The creator talks about rents and how hard life is for young people.

qa.q: What might Kiran get from the videos, and what suggests it is not all positive?
qa.a: Kiran seems to feel understood and thrilled, grinning and repeating the sharpest lines, but afterwards is wound up and snappy, though Salma cannot be sure what Kiran thinks.

qa.q: What question did Salma ask, and why is it useful?
qa.a: "Who makes money when you're angry?" helps Kiran see whether the creator profits from outrage, so Kiran can keep the good ideas while questioning the anger.

qa.q: How does Salma see Kiran's admiration?
qa.a: Salma sees real value in the rent points but worries about the anger they stir, and holds these as observations, not certainties.

grounding: Kiran admires a loud creator who voices Kiran's feelings and thrills at his attacks, while an observer notes the anger he feeds and the value of his ideas.

passage:
Tenzin, you think I don't understand your phone? Listen. When I was twenty-one, I was Minakshi the college girl then, not your boring aunty. There was a man on a local radio call-in show every night. He shouted what we all felt about the corruption at the ration shops. When he named people and called them rats, my friends and I cheered at the hostel radio. I felt brave just listening.

Then one night he named our warden, a kind woman who had lent me bus fare. He had no proof. The next week he started selling his cassettes of "the best insults".

That stopped me. I still agreed about the ration shops. But I began asking: who gains when I am angry? I kept his good points and switched him off when he was just feeding on rage.

qa.q: What did the radio man start selling?
qa.a: He started selling cassettes of "the best insults".

qa.q: How did young Minakshi feel when she listened to the radio show?
qa.a: Young Minakshi felt brave and excited, cheering with friends because he voiced their anger.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed how Minakshi listened?
qa.a: When he attacked the kind warden without proof and then sold insult cassettes, she began asking who gains from her anger.

qa.q: How might the warden have felt being named on the show?
qa.a: The warden would likely have felt hurt and unfairly shamed, since she was kind and there was no proof.

grounding: The elder's story shows a young woman thrilled by a loud voice who keeps his ideas but questions how he profits from anger.

passage:
Exam week, and the hostel Wi-Fi died every evening, so Omkar rationed his data for one thing: the videos of a creator who called himself the Straight Talker. The man said exactly what Omkar felt about unfair entrance exams, and when he tore apart some official, Omkar's heart raced. He shared every clip.

On Thursday his roommate Tenzin, studying under a torch during the power cut, said, "Watch his last three. Count how many times he says 'buy the course'." Omkar laughed it off, then counted anyway. Seven. After each attack came a link to a paid crash course.

Omkar stared at the dim screen. The ideas about exam fairness still made sense. But the anger felt different now, like something being sold to him. He unfollowed, saved two videos he genuinely found useful, and went back to his notes.

qa.q: How many times did the creator say "buy the course" in the last three videos?
What was Omkar feeling after he counted the links?
qa.a: Omkar felt uneasy and a little used, sensing that the anger he enjoyed was being sold to him.

qa.q: What balanced choice did Omkar make, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Omkar kept the two useful videos but unfollowed, holding on to good ideas while stepping away from someone profiting from outrage.

qa.q: How might Tenzin see the creator compared with Omkar at the start?
qa.a: Tenzin sees a seller using anger to push a course, while Omkar at first saw a hero voicing his own frustration.

grounding: The story shows a young man thrilled by a loud creator who notices the creator profits from outrage and questions him while keeping useful ideas.
